items.title: [popsci.com] Nearby giant likely tilted hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, about 1,000 light-years away, stopped transiting its star in March 2026 because the gravitational pull of a nearby, still-unseen planet tilted its orbit out of Earth’s line of sight. NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days. Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner.

items.title: [tuoitre.vn] European Hera probe begins examining asteroid struck in NASA deflection test
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has begun surveying the Didymos asteroid pair from about 25 to 30 kilometers away, four years after NASA deliberately struck the smaller asteroid, Dimorphos, to test asteroid deflection. Hera’s first images show Didymos from a new angle, revealing boulders, craters and ridge-like features; some rocks may have been blasted from Dimorphos and traveled about 1 kilometer to the larger asteroid. The 2022 impact shortened Dimorphos’ orbit around Didymos by about 32 to 33 minutes and also altered the pair’s path around the sun. Hera’s close-up investigation aims to determine how the impact changed Dimorphos and why the deflection was greater than simulations predicted. The probe is expected to begin closer, more detailed observations next month, using 25 instruments and two CubeSats that will survey Dimorphos and attempt to land there.

items.title: [phys.org] COP31 nations split over 1.5°C goal as threshold nears
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Halfway through the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, countries are divided over whether to keep the 1.5°C warming limit as a central goal after the United Nations said in September that crossing it was imminent and unavoidable. Global temperatures have risen about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. Some countries want the summit’s final decision to reaffirm 1.5°C as the “right goal” and call for temperatures to return below that limit as soon as possible. Other negotiators, including members of the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, are pushing to weaken or remove references to the target. Scientists say reversing an overshoot would require sharp emissions cuts and large-scale carbon removal over decades; University of Exeter climate scientist Pierre Friedlingstein described that prospect as “extremely ambitious”.

items.title: [newspaceeconomy.ca] Researchers test AI systems for satellite servicing, imaging and astronomy
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Three research efforts are testing autonomous decision-making for space operations, from analyzing Earth imagery in orbit to guiding satellite rescues and scheduling astronomical observations. Planet Labs’ Pelican-4 satellite used an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin processor to detect aircraft in imagery in March. Google Research and Planet Labs said a prototype later ran the Gemma 4 model on an orbital tensor-processing unit. A team led by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign is developing CORTEX, software to plan and guide a servicing spacecraft’s approach to an unresponsive satellite. A separate astronomical-survey challenge evaluated systems submitted by 102 teams in simulated observing campaigns. Researchers found that leading entries combined numerical exposure planning with language models, while changes to science priorities substantially changed the systems’ rankings.

items.title: [oglobo.globo.com] El Niño threatens harvests as Peru warns millions face flood risk
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An exceptionally strong 2026–27 El Niño is disrupting food production and prompting emergency measures. Peru declared an emergency across more than 70% of its municipalities over flood danger, with authorities warning that more than 9 million people face a high risk of floods and landslides. In the Philippines, unmilled rice production fell 18% in the three months to September, while forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November. Nearly 896,000 hectares have burned in Indonesia since January; smoke has led to school closures and respiratory illness, according to a report citing BBC. Cereal maker Kellanova has also changed the ingredients in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops sold in the UK and Europe, citing weather-related problems with the availability and quality of rice and grains. The UN’s International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) says overlapping climate and economic shocks could cost the global economy as much as $11 trillion, with energy and fertilizer costs adding pressure across food systems. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in September it had received only one-fifth of the $202 million requested to prepare for food crises in 22 high-risk countries.

items.title: [abc7news.com] Record-strength El Niño and early polar vortex disruption complicate winter outlook
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The U.S. National Weather Service’s Climate Prediction Center said a strong-to-very-strong El Niño is likely to persist through January–March 2027. It put the chance of the event exceeding all El Niños recorded since 1950 at roughly 60% for the October–December and November–January periods. Ocean temperatures in the central equatorial Pacific were about 2.5 degrees Celsius above average, and forecasters said the event could strengthen further into early next year. The polar vortex — high-altitude winds that usually keep Arctic air near the pole — has weakened and reversed unusually early. The resulting sudden stratospheric warming can increase the chance of Arctic air moving south, but scientists say its timing and overlap with El Niño make the winter difficult to predict. The latest cold spell in parts of the United States and Europe is expected to ease. Forecasters expect a stronger southern storm track to increase rain and flood risks in parts of the South and West, while much of the northern United States may be warmer and less snowy than usual. California could see atmospheric rivers, coastal flooding and landslides, while warmer temperatures could reduce mountain snowpack in the Northwest. El Niño’s strongest effects are expected from December through February, and NOAA’s outlook extends through March.

items.content_html:

items.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

🔭 ✏️

The FBI warned on Nov. 13 that hackers have used ARTEX, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework, since at least August to automate intrusions against organizations in sectors including finance, government, technology and health care. The framework uses AI agents to perform tasks ranging from reconnaissance to data theft, and some attackers gained privileged access in under three hours, the bureau said. The FBI cited the ConnectWise Cloud Backup breach, in which attackers used compromised application identities to attempt logins to more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 tenants; those attempts do not establish that attackers stole data from every tenant. In a separate campaign, Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 said attackers used a customized version of the Cairn framework in 25 operations against at least 19 organizations in August and September, gaining unauthorized access or retrieving data at 10 of them. The FBI urged organizations to restrict application permissions, monitor authentication and cloud activity, and secure internet-facing systems.

items.title: [traficom.fi] Cyberattacks disrupt refrigeration, water and energy control systems
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Cyber incidents targeting operational technology (OT) systems—the controllers that monitor and operate physical equipment—have disrupted refrigeration, water and energy operations, often through exposed or outdated devices. Attacks on European supermarket refrigeration systems caused food spoilage, while incidents affecting U.S. water utilities and Polish energy organizations disrupted monitoring and control. French industry estimates put food waste and structural damage from the refrigeration attacks at tens of millions of euros. Isolating a compromised system can cut operators off from equipment-status information they need to make safe decisions, according to a Communications of the ACM contributor. Finland’s Transport and Communications Agency said household smart devices were not targets in the European refrigeration attacks, but advised users to secure routers and connected devices.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

items.title: [thehackernews.com] Hackers use 4,837 hijacked GitHub accounts to steal continuous integration secrets
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A campaign dubbed wfx-loot used stolen credentials from 4,837 GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 repositories and plant code designed to steal developer and cloud secrets. Security researchers confirmed the payload ran in at least 1,806 repositories. A separate analysis counted malicious commits in 8,093 public repositories, but that does not mean the code executed in each one. The attackers tested access with pull requests titled “docs: dependency audit notes,” then briefly inserted a roughly 1,500-line script into GitHub Actions workflows or npm installation hooks. The script sought GitHub, cloud, package-publishing and AI-service credentials. Attackers often reverted the changes and deleted workflow logs. The campaign relied on valid stolen account tokens, not a flaw in GitHub Actions. Researchers said the operation was still active on Nov. 12, with new probe requests and malicious code still appearing. They advised repository owners to revoke compromised access, rotate every secret available to affected workflows and check cloud accounts for persistent access.

items.title: [abcnews.com] International student enrollment at U.S. colleges falls 9% as visa uncertainty grows
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges fell 15% this fall, while total international enrollment dropped 9%, according to a preliminary survey of more than 800 institutions by the Institute of International Education. The declines mark a second consecutive year of losses: new enrollment fell 18% last year, and total enrollment fell 3%. College leaders cited visa uncertainty, travel restrictions and competition from universities abroad; high U.S. tuition also weighs on students’ choices. The Trump administration has proposed a $70,000 fee for each international student a college recommends for Optional Practical Training (OPT), a post-study work program. The Institute of International Education found that 95% of surveyed institutions expect students to consider another country if OPT is unavailable. The Department of Homeland Security has not set a timetable for finalizing the fee proposal, which universities say could face legal challenges.
